job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Loophole and drafting review of S. 2817 (manager's amendment of Oct. 6, 2026)

Items run in section order, then cross-cutting gaps. If amendment time is limited, I'd prioritize **#10-12** (grandfather clause), **#14-15** (environmental assessment exemption), **#22** (the sunset), **#16-17** (enforceability of §4/§5), and **#6-8** (who counts as a "U.S. person" and the single-vessel threshold).

## Section 2: Definitions

1. **§2(1)(A), single-vessel test.** The 10,000 t/yr threshold applies per vessel, so an operator can run several vessels, each under the line, or spread them across affiliates. There is no aggregation rule for vessels or commonly controlled entities.

2. **§2(1)(A), threshold level.** Anything under 10,000 t/yr per vessel is lawful, which leaves room for large pilot or "test" operations. Consider a much lower threshold, or a ban on any commercial-purpose recovery regardless of volume.

3. **§2(1)(A), undefined measurement terms.** "Per year" (calendar or rolling), wet versus dry weight (nodules carry significant water), "recovery" (collected, lifted, or landed), and "other mineral resources" (crusts, sulfides, sediments) are all undefined. Each is a litigable way to fall under the threshold.

4. **§2(1)(A), the 200-meter test.** "Seabed" is undefined, and it is unclear whether depth is measured at the point of recovery or across the site. Shallower sites such as seamount summits fall outside the definition. The 200 m line also doesn't match the "deep seabed" title.

5. **§2(1)(B), "Secretary" is undefined.** Nothing in §2 says which Secretary (Commerce? Interior?). §6 names the Secretary of State specifically, so context doesn't resolve it.

6. **§2(1)(B), standardless discretion.** "Comparable" risk has no criteria, procedure, deadline, or publication requirement, and the Secretary is never required to act. Because criminal liability under §5(b) could depend on it, expect vagueness, fair-notice, nondelegation, and APA challenges. A future administration could also simply never use it.

7. **§2(2), "U.S. person" is narrow.** It omits foreign subsidiaries of U.S. companies, partnerships, LLCs, trusts, and unincorporated associations (the text says "corporation"). Without a definition of "State," it also leaves out D.C. and the territories, and it has no ownership-or-control test. Reincorporating a mining arm abroad could take it outside §3(a).

8. **§2(3), "covered vessel."** Vessels of 5,000 gross tons or less, platforms, support, transport, and processing ships, and vessels whose collection gear is installed later all escape §4. The definition may also catch unrelated seabed dredgers (for example sand and gravel), which invites an overbreadth objection.

9. **§2, missing definitions.** "Person," "operator," "United States," "State," "engage in," and "exploration license" are undefined. Each is a point where defendants can argue the statute doesn't reach them.

## Section 3: Prohibition

10. **§3(b), scope of the grandfather clause.** Exploration licenses don't authorize commercial extraction, so "mining conducted under an exploration license" is ambiguous. It can be read to allow open-ended recovery by anyone holding such a license, with no cap on volume, area, or duration and no conditions.

11. **§3(b), which licenses count.** The text isn't limited to U.S.-issued licenses, so licenses issued by foreign states or sponsored through the ISA and held by U.S. persons could qualify. It also doesn't bar renewal, extension, modification, expansion, or transfer of covered licenses.

12. **§3(b), cutoff date.** "Before the date of enactment" invites a rush of license issuance and applications before the bill passes. Pending applications are not addressed. Consider an earlier cutoff (such as introduction) and an express statement that pending applications are void.

13. **§3(a), territorial reach.** "In the United States" is undefined, so it's unclear whether it covers the territorial sea, EEZ, outer continental shelf, extended continental shelf, or territories. Foreign persons and foreign-flag vessels operating on the U.S. shelf may fall outside it, and "person in the United States" is unclear for remote operations.

14. **§3(a), narrow conduct covered.** Only the act of recovery is prohibited. Processing, transport, sale, import, financing, insurance, chartering, and equipment supply are not, and there is no attempt, conspiracy, or aiding-and-abetting language. Foreign-flag or foreign-subsidiary mining could feed U.S. processing legally.

15. **§3(c), environmental assessment exemption is open-ended.** "Activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment" is undefined and has no cap on volume, area, or duration. It also requires no government-approved plan, independent oversight, or notice, and it depends on a subjective "purpose" that is hard to disprove.

16. **§3(c), no bar on selling recovered material.** Nothing prevents an "assessment" operation from selling or stockpiling what it lifts. That makes the exemption a possible cover for commercial-scale activity.

17. **§3, relationship to existing law.** The bill doesn't amend or repeal the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. § 1401 et seq.) or OCSLA, and it has no "notwithstanding any other law" clause. NOAA could keep issuing licenses and permits, and permit holders would argue authorization or conflict. Counsel should confirm the right statutory hooks.

## Section 4: Registry

18. **§4, no enforcement.** §5 penalizes only violations of §3, so failure to register or file reports has no express penalty. A false certification would depend on general false-statement law.

19. **§4(a), thin registration terms.** There is no deadline, no required content (ownership, flag, equipment, operating area), no rulemaking authority, and no public access. "Operator" is undefined, so a shell entity could be named as operator.

20. **§4(b), self-certified and unverifiable.** Reports are certified by the operator, with no authority to inspect, audit, require position tracking (AIS), place observers, or demand records. Contents aren't specified (tonnage, wet or dry, location, depth), so reports may not prove whether the threshold was crossed.

## Section 5: Penalties

21. **§5(a), date conflict.** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §8 delays effectiveness by 180 days. Defendants will argue no violation can occur before the effective date, or raise fair-notice problems. Tie it to the effective date.

22. **§5(a), no procedure.** The bill doesn't say who assesses, adjudicates, or collects penalties, what notice and hearing apply, or what factors guide the amount. Administrative assessment could draw a Seventh Amendment challenge under *SEC v. Jarkesy* (2024), so a district-court action by the Attorney General is safer.

23. **§5, thin remedies.** There is no injunctive relief, seizure or forfeiture of vessels, equipment, and minerals, disgorgement, port-access denial, or restoration liability. A "not more than" $1M/day cap may be lower than revenue for a large operation.

24. **§5(b), "willfully" is undefined.** It may be read to require knowledge that the conduct was unlawful, which, combined with ambiguous exemptions and §2(1)(B), hands defendants a strong defense. There is also no responsible-corporate-officer language and no criminal coverage for §4 violations such as false reports.

## Sections 6-8: Diplomacy, duration, effective date

25. **§6, soft and ambiguous.** "Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months" doesn't say whether the deadline applies to starting or finishing talks, and "seek" is not judicially enforceable. There is no reporting to Congress, no consequence for missing the deadline, and no definition of "equivalent."

26. **§7(a), undefined "serious harm" and no process.** There is no burden of proof or precautionary standard. The bill also doesn't say who commissions or funds the National Academies report, when it is due, what it must find, or whether Congress is bound by it. It's also unclear whether the joint resolution lifts the ban on its own.

27. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), internal conflict.** §7(a) says the ban lasts until Congress finds mining safe, while §7(b) ends the Act after 10 years regardless. A court would likely treat the specific sunset as controlling, which makes the §7(a) safeguard meaningless.

28. **§7(b), the sunset reverses the default.** After 10 years the ban lapses automatically with no review, report, or vote, so industry can wait it out. Because of the 180-day delay, the effective ban lasts only about 9.5 years.

29. **§7(b), no savings clause.** Nothing preserves enforcement of violations that occurred before the sunset, so defendants may argue pending or past violations abate when the Act expires.

30. **§8, 180-day window.** Operators can ramp up, finalize licenses, or move assets offshore during the gap. There is no interim bar on new licenses or permits and no wind-down rule. The bill also uses two triggers (enactment and effective date) inconsistently, as in #12 and #21.

## Cross-cutting gaps

31. **No designated enforcing agency.** The bill never says who enforces §3 (NOAA, Commerce, DOJ, Coast Guard). It gives no rulemaking, investigation, boarding, seizure, or subpoena authority and authorizes no appropriations, so the prohibition could go unenforced.

32. **No citizen-suit or judicial-review provision.** If an agency declines to enforce, outside groups have no way to sue. Consider a citizen-suit clause with fee-shifting, modeled on ESA §11(g), and review of the §2(1)(B) determinations.

33. **No severability clause.** If a court strikes §2(1)(B), the extraterritorial reach, or another provision, the rest of the Act is left exposed or inoperative.

34. **No findings, purpose, or constitutional-authority statement.** This weakens the record for defending the bill and for reading ambiguities narrowly against exemptions.

35. **Extraterritorial friction.** "U.S. person anywhere" will run into operations licensed by other states within their own waters, which invites comity and international-law objections. The bill also gives no practical means to obtain evidence or reach assets abroad.

I'm not a substitute for legal counsel. The statutory citations (DSHMRA, OCSLA, *Jarkesy*, ESA §11(g)) and my reading of how they interact with the bill should be confirmed by CADM's counsel or the Hill staff drafters before they go into amendment language. I can turn the priority items into proposed amendment text or a one-page memo for Commerce Committee staff if you'd like.
